Chapter 2: Relearning Hunger and Fullness Signals
Now that those old diet rules are starting to loosen their grip, it’s time to turn your attention inward—back to your body’s own signals of hunger and fullness. For a lot of us, these cues have gotten pretty muted, maybe even ignored, after years of following strict routines or external advice. Relearning them is gentle and honestly, kind of profound—like tuning up a guitar that’s been sitting in the corner, out of tune for ages.
Hunger is a basic biological signal, just as real and important as the need for sleep or fresh air. But in a culture that glorifies willpower and self-denial, hunger sometimes gets treated like an enemy—something to suppress or ignore. Maybe you’ve learned to distrust your hunger, worried that if you answer its call, you’ll end up overeating or losing control.
So, how do you start reconnecting with hunger? It begins with noticing the early signs. Hunger isn’t always a growling stomach—it could be irritability, trouble focusing, or just feeling drained. By pausing and checking in with yourself throughout the day, you can start to tell the difference between a gentle nudge and that desperate, ravenous hunger that can leave you eating past the point of comfort.
There’s a simple way to picture this: imagine a scale from one to ten. One means you’re painfully hungry, and ten is when you’re uncomfortably full. The sweet spot is somewhere in the middle—not letting yourself get too empty or too stuffed. It’s about noticing those subtle shifts, and responding before things get extreme.
Fullness is another signal that’s worth tuning into. Diets often teach us to ignore fullness—whether it’s eating past comfort during those so-called “cheat” moments, or stopping short of satisfaction because of fear. But intuitive eating invites you to do something different: eat with awareness, and pause every now and then to check in with how you’re feeling.
Here are some gentle ways to practice tuning in:
Before you eat, take a moment and ask yourself, “What does hunger feel like right now?” Is it physical, emotional, or maybe a bit of both?
While you’re eating, slow down just enough to really notice the taste and texture of your food. This isn’t about being perfect—it’s just about making space for awareness.
About halfway through your meal, pause and check in: “How does my body feel right now? Am I satisfied, or do I need a little more?”
And when you’re finished, notice how your body feels. Is there a sense of comfort, an energy boost, or maybe some sluggishness?
Remember, this process isn’t about getting it right every time. It’s about building trust with yourself. Over time, as you keep practicing, your body’s signals will become a lot clearer—and eating will shift from being all about rules to being about real attunement.
Of course, there will be moments when old habits pop up or things feel uncertain. That’s okay. Each meal is just another chance to listen and learn.
Let’s bring it to life with a couple of real-world examples. Imagine someone who’s spent years skipping breakfast to “save calories.” They start to notice that those mid-morning headaches and bouts of irritability are actually signs of hunger. Once they start honoring that signal with a nourishing breakfast, their energy and mood improve—and the urge to overeat later in the day starts to fade.
Or picture someone who’s always cleaned their plate, no matter how full they felt. Now, they try pausing halfway through a meal. Sometimes, their body says, “That’s enough.” Other times, it needs a little more. The key is to approach all of this with curiosity, not judgment.
Relearning hunger and fullness is a gradual journey, and it calls for patience and self-kindness. But it’s really the foundation for building a peaceful, trusting relationship with food—and with yourself.
